title: John Marrero and Puy Saville banjo rivalry
summary: Verrett recalls Marrero and Saville, from Natchez, cutting heads at the Pelican and heard from the Music Box.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Did you ever hear John Marrero in the old days? How was he?

Well I heard him. He was a good banjo player too. John Marrero, he was a good man. And him, I heard him. Like I told you, this guy, a banjo player, Pujic Saville. Oh yeah, I heard George Dino talk about him.
He was a good man. Oh yeah.
That guy can pick more banjo, you know, just pick. Vary at highest his size, with the clarinet he makes, all that, you know, he's wonderful. Played a lot of single string work there?
What do you do, do you play with bands much? What do you do?
The most I heard of him, he's been at the music box, you see?

At the music box, he'd wait there every night, I was at the farm to basically go take a walk. You can hear him picking for about two blocks. The music box was upstairs, you can hear him. He was a wonderful banjo. He's a one-on-one, you know he used to have these, like at the Pelican they'd have a band here and a band there, opposite. Yeah. Well they used to call themselves cutting heads, you see. It would be John Marrera and Puy Saville. John couldn't pick no banjo with him. That man was terrific. He was from Natchez, Mississippi. He was terrific. The only guy without picking was Rennie Hall. Rennie Hall had a keen style of picking, fast, much faster than everything else. He'd make everything any trumpet player make, any clarinet, any saxophone player make. He'd make it on the banjo, Rennie Hall. He's known for that. Anybody, you know anybody, you know. In those days, I tell you, he was the best.
